newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk government MPs face probe over crash scandal.
newsitem.headline: Turk government MPs face probe over crash scandal.

text.p: Two deputies in Turkey's coalition government face possible criminal charges over a scandal linking the state and underworld gangs, according to a report presented on Friday by the Turkish Justice Ministry.

"The government has fulfilled its duty and after completing the investigation in an administrative sense, passed it on to the judicial authorities," Justice Minister Sevket Kazan told a news conference.

Former interior minister Mehmet Agar and MP Sedat Bucak are among 35 people targeted for investigation in a report ordered by Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan after a car crash in which a wanted gangster and a top policeman died in the same car.
Agar and Bucak are both members of Tansu Ciller's True Path Party which formed a coalition last June with Erbakan's Islamist Welfare Party.
Bucak, a government MP leading a Kurdish clan paid by the state to fight separatist Kurdish rebels, survived the crash on November 3 with minor injuries.
A fortnight later Erbakan commissioned a committee to produce the report, which also called for 85 people to be questioned as witnesses about the events leading to the unlikely group sharing a car.
Agar, who quit as interior minister in November, is to be investigated over the signing of a false police document for Abdullah Catli, the gangster who died in the crash.

Kazan said his ministry would approve any prosecutor's request to lift the MPs' immunity from prosecution. In December, the Justice Ministry rejected a prosecutor's report calling for Agar's immunity to be lifted.
Bucak is to be investigated on a charge of concealing Catli, who was allegedly used by officials to kill Turkey's political opponents.
A parliamentary commission is also expected to produce a report on the incident after a four-month investigation.

The prime ministry report also call for an investigation into former Turkish police chief Agar and various security officials in connection with the murder of Turkey's "casino king" Omer Lutfi Topal last year.

The media and opposition have alleged that leading officials directed hit squads to kill Kurdish rebel sympathisers and business rivals. More than 1,300 people have died since 1992 in unsolved political killings, human rights activists say.
